analysis.one_liner: Raises the royalty rates, rents, and fees oil and gas companies pay to drill on federal public lands.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to raise the federal onshore oil and gas royalty from 12.5% to 18.75% never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee from March 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made oil and gas companies pay more to drill on land owned by the public: the royalty they pay on each barrel would rise from 12.5% to 18.75%, the minimum bid to buy a federal lease would rise from $2 to $10 per acre, and annual rent would double. It would also add a new fee for companies that ask to have public land opened to drilling, and require the Interior Department to raise all these charges with inflation every four years. The extra money would flow to the federal treasury and, through the existing revenue-sharing formula, to state governments.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and state governments would collect a larger share of the value of oil and gas taken from publicly owned land. The bill also directs a study of whether the Interior Department is properly collecting and auditing those payments.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the royalty rate on onshore federal oil and gas from 12.5% to 18.75%, increasing the public's share of the value of oil and gas taken from land it owns.

Raises the minimum acceptable bid for a federal lease from $2 to $10 per acre and doubles annual rental rates (from $1.50 to $3 per acre in the first years, and from $2 to $5 thereafter), so companies pay closer to fair market value to lock up public acreage.
Creates a new fee of at least $15 per acre for anyone who nominates public land for oil and gas leasing, covering processing costs that taxpayers currently absorb.

Requires the Interior Department to adjust all these rates and fees for inflation at least every four years, so they stop eroding over time, and to raise them further when needed to ensure a fair return to the United States.

Directs the Comptroller General to arrange a National Academy of Sciences study, with a report to Congress within three to five years, on whether Interior's systems for collecting and auditing oil and gas payments are working and whether the government is capturing full value for the public.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies producing on federal land would pay higher royalties, rents, bids, and fees. Some of that cost could be passed on to consumers through somewhat higher energy prices, or shift drilling to state and private land where rates and rules differ.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers on federal land

drawbacks.text: The bill directly raises production costs on federal land: a company would pay 18.75% of the value of production instead of 12.5%, plus higher rents, bids, and fees, which companies could pass through to consumers or use as a reason to shift drilling off federal lands.

The new $15-per-acre fee for merely nominating land for leasing could discourage interest in federal lease sales, reducing the volume of leasing and potentially the revenue the higher rates are meant to raise.
The bill sets no specific use for the added revenue and relies on a study, three to five years after enactment, to determine whether the new rates actually capture full value for the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a larger, inflation-proofed return on publicly owned minerals plus a real audit of collection systems — falls on taxpayers broadly, while the cost falls on a specific industry that has paid the same 12.5% rate for a century. The main honest concerns are modest pass-through to energy prices and the possibility that steeper costs push production and its economic benefits onto state and private land, weakening what federal rates can capture.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jacky Rosen introduced the bill on March 9, 2021, joined by Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever recorded for the rest of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land are better off: the 12.5% royalty, $2 minimum bid, and low rental rates all stayed exactly where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers on federal land

for.name: Sen. Jacky Rosen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its only Democratic cosponsor.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the sponsorship bipartisan.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee leadership (Chair Joe Manchin)
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee with no action from referral in March 2021 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Nevada Democrat and one Iowa Republican — but with only two cosponsors total and no vote ever taken, no partisan pattern was ever tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies producing on federal lands
industries.note: The bill would have ended a century-old bargain in which these companies pay a 12.5% royalty — the rate set in 1920 — to extract publicly owned oil and gas, replacing it with an 18.75% royalty plus higher bids, rents, and fees, all adjusted for inflation. Their interest in keeping the old rates runs directly against the public's interest in full market value for its own resources.

The new fee for nominating public land for leasing and the study of valuation methods would change how lease speculation on federal acreage is priced, raising the cost of parking speculative claims but leaving the brokerage role intact.
